lead: "The agent answered 4,000 messages" doesn't tell you whether the company gained anything. Really measuring means comparing against the number from before, on the same scale, and also looking at what may have gotten worse. At 30, 60, and 90 days the question changes: does it work, is it stable, was it worth the money?
objetivo: build a dashboard of 3 indicators with before-and-after values and run the 30-, 60-, and 90-day reviews against the baseline.

aprende.t: The three indicators: result, operation, and safeguard
Vanity metrics and the target that teaches people to cheat
What you ask at 30, 60, and 90 days
ROI and payback in owner's language

hero_alt: Tablet with a line chart next to two printed sheets with bar charts, a ruler, and a pencil.

secoes.sub: One of each type, always with the before value. Click each one.

nos.detalhe: Closed sale, margin, order delivered on time, cost per order. Slow to move, but it's what pays for the project. At Horizonte: orders closed from a quote sent.
Response time, time per task, the day's queue. It moves in days and shows whether the agent is being used. On its own, it misleads.
Pricing error, complaints, average discount, rework, data incident. If operations improve and protection gets worse, the gain is false.
Each indicator has its value from before the agent, measured the same way, in the same type of period. Without it, the dashboard only shows movement.

secoes.legenda: Weekly or monthly frequency, never daily: Monday has a backlog and Friday has people leaving early.
secoes.dica: Lab counterexample (F11): the Horizonte dashboard shows messages answered and conversations started, with no baseline column and no sales or complaints.

secoes.sub: Each review answers a different question.

texto: End of the pilot. Is the agent being used? Did operations improve against the baseline? Did any protection get worse?
Fix the usage friction: where the team gives up, where they go back to the old way. Decision: continue, adjust, or stop.

exemplo.texto: Usage dropping in the third week: the process didn't fit into the routine. Go back to the diagnosis.

texto: Did the gain hold without the consultant around? Does the real cost per task match what you calculated in lesson 4? Did errors go down, or just move somewhere else?
Compare the gain estimated at the start with the real one.

exemplo.texto: "If I disappear for a month, does this keep working?"

texto: Now the result indicator has had time to move. Calculate the ROI and the payback, and decide: expand to another team, keep it as it is, or turn it off.
What you measured becomes the baseline for the next cycle.

exemplo.texto: "We invested R$ X, we earn R$ Y per month, the money comes back in Z months."

texto: An indicator on its own becomes a target: response time drops because people answer anything; support closes tickets without solving them; discounts go up to close a sale.
That's why each operations indicator goes together with a protection one. And the dashboard shows adoption: how many people use it per week.

exemplo.texto: Response time (operations) + quotes with the wrong price (protection).

secoes.sub: One row per indicator. Paste it into a spreadsheet and update it at the agreed frequency.

blocos.conteudo:
DASHBOARD · <company> · <process> · baseline measured on <date> by <who>

| Type | Metric | How it's measured (source, who counts) | Before | 30 days | 60 days | 90 days | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Result | <closed orders / quotes> | <sales spreadsheet, Patrícia> | <...> | | | | <...> |
| Operation | <median time to quote> | <50 orders, intake time x send time> | <...> | | | | <...> |
| Protection | <quotes with the wrong price> | <weekly check> | <...> | | | | <don't get worse> |
| Adoption | <people who used it this week> | <agent log> | 0 | | | | <...> |
| Cost | <real cost per task (R$)> | <invoice + review minutes> | — | | | | <<= calculated> |

REVIEW 30: does it work? | REVIEW 60: is it stable? | REVIEW 90: was it worth it? -> [expand] [keep] [turn off]

Monthly gain (R$)  = (value before - value after) x volume x unit cost
                     (e.g.: minutes saved x orders x cost per minute)
Monthly cost (R$)  = tool + tokens + human review + maintenance
Investment (R$)    = diagnosis + pilot + rollout (one time)

Yearly ROI (%)     = (monthly gain x 12 - monthly cost x 12 - investment)
                     / (monthly cost x 12 + investment) x 100
Payback (months)   = investment / (monthly gain - monthly cost)

Use the MEASURED gain (dashboard), not the estimated one. If monthly gain <= monthly cost, there is no payback: the project doesn't pay for itself.

abas.html:
• Operation: median time to quote from 3 h 40 min → 50 min.
  • Protection: quotes with a wrong price from 8% → 6%.
  • Result: orders closed from quotes from 31% → 35%.
  • Adoption: 5 of 6 salespeople using it every week.

Investment R$ 18k; measured gain R$ 9k/month; cost R$ 2k/month. Payback = 18 ÷ (9 − 2) ≈ 2.6 months. ROI for the year = (108 − 24 − 18) ÷ (24 + 18) ≈ 157%.

Illustrative numbers, for practicing the math.

• Vanity metric: messages answered and conversations started measure motion, not results.
  • No "before" column: the period starts on the day the agent was turned on (this is failure F11 from the lab).
  • Changing the yardstick: measuring before by sample and after by the system gives numbers that can't be compared.
  • ROI with the estimated gain: on day 90, use the measured one.

secoes.sub: Start from the lab's dashboard, which has failure F11.

exercicios.texto: In the lab, open Horizonte's metrics dashboard. List what it measures, what is missing (baseline, result, protection), and why no one knows whether the agent helped.
exercicios.pronto: you wrote, in up to 5 lines, why the current dashboard proves nothing.

exercicios.texto: Build the 30/60/90 dashboard for the lesson 5 pilot: one result metric, one operation metric, and one protection metric, with how to measure it and the before value (real from the lab, or simulated, marked as a simulation).
exercicios.pronto: the dashboard has 3 metrics with before and after values filled in, and a line saying who measures and where the number comes from.

exercicios.texto: Using the numbers from your dashboard and an estimated investment, calculate ROI and payback, and write the sentence for Carlos in owner's language.
exercicios.pronto: the sentence fits in two lines and has the amount invested, the monthly gain, and the payback period.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: The dashboard shows "4,000 messages answered this month". What is missing?
opcoes: The before value and a result and protection metric.
The name of the model used.
perguntas.explica: It's a vanity metric: it measures motion. Without a baseline and without a result (sale, margin) or protection (complaints), it doesn't prove a gain.

perguntas.p: Response time was cut in half, but price complaints doubled. Conclusion?
opcoes: The gain is false: a protection got worse; adjust or stop.
perguntas.explica: An operation metric on its own teaches people to cheat. If protection gets worse, the result doesn't hold up.

perguntas.p: Investment of R$ 12k, measured gain of R$ 5k/month, cost of R$ 1k/month. Payback?
perguntas.explica: Payback = investment ÷ (gain − cost) = 12 ÷ (5 − 1) = 3 months. The common mistake is forgetting to subtract the monthly cost.

perguntas.p: Why measure weekly or monthly, and not daily?
opcoes: Because each day has its own variation (pile-up on Monday, a shorter Friday) that muddles the comparison.
Because the system doesn't allow it.
perguntas.explica: Short periods mix the agent's effect with the normal variation of the week.

itens.texto: Result, operation, and protection, always with the before value and the same yardstick.
Does it work? Is it stable? Was it worth the money? Then: expand, keep, or turn it off.
Motion is not a result. Operation goes hand in hand with protection.
